newsitem.title: USA: NYC stresses new underwriters must pay taxes.
newsitem.headline: NYC stresses new underwriters must pay taxes.

text.p: New York City, which started selecting investment bankers for lucrative spots on its underwriting team for a new agency, emphasized that the companies and top officials must have paid their taxes.

City officials, who declined to be named, said that this requirement reflects its past experience with financial companies and some of their employees, who either failed to comply or were involved in disputes.

In its request for proposals from underwriters, who will be competing fiercely for the new spots, the city said: "The selection will be based primarily on an analysis of the responding firms' ability to provide the highest quality investment banking and marketing services as well as a firm's demonstrated willingness to resolove prior and ongoing disputes with the City of New York and its related entities and the compliance of firm employees with city tax requirements."

City officials said the employees being targeted are managing directors, partners and similar officers. They noted the decision to emphasize tax compliance was due to problems New York City has had with more than one financial firm.

PaineWebber early this year got a tax liability knocked out because the city failed to serve notice properly. City officials said the matter was being negotiated. A PaineWebber spokesman had no information immediately available to comment.

The new underwriting team was expected to be selected by May or June, a city official added, noting that the city also reserved the right to reshuffle its teams for its own general obligation debt and for bonds sold by the Municipal Water Finance Authority due to the selections made for the new agency, the New York City Transitional Financing Authority.

The city's request for proposals for the first time since January 1994 includes questions on how underwriters would be compensated for their work, another city official said. The document asked underwriters whether their fee should be higher for the first financing by the new authority than for subsequent debt sales.
